quote_zh: Nick’s ‘scornful solidarity’ is a belated allegiance, forged only after Gatsby is dead and the world has abandoned him. The word carries political and moral weight, suggesting a principled stand against the Buchanans’ carelessness. This solidarity is both a rebuke and an elegy; it comes too late to save Gatsby but it salvages Nick’s own moral vision. Fitzgerald uses the term to elevate Nick’s loyalty above mere sympathy, casting it as a defiant, ethical commitment.
ex_en: The solidarity that emerged among Gatsby’s few mourners was a frail but defiant counterpoint to the vast silence of his former guests.
ex_zh: The old oaks in the forest shared an unspoken solidarity, their roots intertwined in a dark, enduring embrace.

def_en: to put off an action or event to a later time; postpone
def_zh: defer to, defer action, defer judgment
quote_en: "all arrangements had been deferred until he came" – Nick Carraway telling Gatsby’s father that the funeral plans were postponed (Chapter 9)
quote_zh: The funeral arrangements are ‘deferred’ for the arrival of Henry Gatz, a small gesture of respect that contrasts with the rush with which the rest of the world moves on. The verb echoes Langston Hughes’s ‘a dream deferred,’ hinting at the larger postponement that defined Gatsby’s life. Gatsby spent years deferring happiness to a future that never arrived; now even his burial is deferred. Fitzgerald uses the word to evoke the cumulative weight of waiting that crushes the American Dream.
ex_en: Gatsby had deferred his own authenticity so long that when the moment came to be real, there was nothing left but a gesture.
ex_zh: The old judge deferred his verdict, letting the silence in the courtroom grow until it became a character in the trial.

def_en: feeling or showing deep and solemn respect
def_zh: reverent tone, reverent attitude, reverent silence
quote_en: "He drew me into his office, remarking in a reverent voice that it was a sad time for all of us, and offered me a cigar." – Nick Carraway describing Meyer Wolfshiem’s pious manner when speaking of Gatsby’s death (Chapter 9)
quote_zh: Wolfshiem’s ‘reverent voice’ is deeply ironic, given his adamant refusal to attend Gatsby’s funeral. The adjective exposes the chasm between performance and sincerity; Wolfshiem speaks of sadness with the tones of a mourner, but his actions betray no genuine grief. Fitzgerald uses this false reverence to indict the criminal and business associates who exploited Gatsby and then fled his corpse. The word contrasts painfully with Nick’s own quiet, untheatrical devotion to Gatsby’s memory.
ex_en: Nick’s reverent description of Gatsby’s smile suggests that, even in failure, there was something sacred about the man’s capacity for hope.
ex_zh: The museum visitors spoke in reverent whispers, as if the paintings could hear and might be offended by the truth.

def_en: the skill of clear and expressive speech, especially of distinct pronunciation and articulation
def_zh: elocution lessons, study elocution, practice elocution
quote_en: "Practice elocution, poise and how to attain it" – From the schedule written in the back of young Jimmy Gatz’s copy of ‘Hopalong Cassidy’ (Chapter 9)
quote_zh: The boy Gatsby’s program of ‘elocution’ is a poignant blueprint of self‑improvement, the discipline by which James Gatz tried to erase his humble voice. The word is doubly ironic because the adult Gatsby’s speech is a patchwork of adopted phrases (‘old sport’) that never quite ring true. Elocution—the art of sounding like someone else—is Gatsby’s great project, yet it also marks his fundamental inauthenticity. Fitzgerald uses this small detail to humanize Gatsby, revealing the earnest, lonely child behind the glittering criminal facade.
ex_en: Gatsby’s elocution was a carefully studied performance, each syllable a brick in the wall between his true self and the world.
ex_zh: The old actor’s elocution still held the power to hush a room, each word a velvet hammer striking the silence.

def_en: not permanent; temporary
def_zh: transitory nature, transitory moment, transitory phenomenon
quote_en: "for a transitory enchanted moment man must have held his breath in the presence of this continent, compelled into an aesthetic contemplation he neither understood nor desired" – Nick Carraway imagining the first Dutch sailors’ awe at the sight of the New World (Chapter 9)
quote_zh: In the novel’s final, visionary passage, ‘transitory’ describes the fleeting instant of pure wonder experienced by the first Europeans. The adjective captures the ephemeral quality of all human aspiration: the green light, Gatsby’s dream, the summer itself are transitory. Fitzgerald uses it to cast an elegiac glow over the entire narrative, insisting that beauty and meaning are inseparable from their impermanence. The transitory nature of Gatsby’s triumph makes his effort both futile and sublime.
ex_en: Gatsby’s triumph over class was transitory, a brief candle flame that the wind of East Egg snuffed out without a thought.
ex_zh: The cherry blossoms were a transitory snow, a pink whisper that the spring wind delivered and the spring wind erased.

def_en: concerned with beauty or the appreciation of beauty
def_zh: aesthetic appeal, aesthetic value, purely aesthetic
quote_en: "for a transitory enchanted moment man must have held his breath in the presence of this continent, compelled into an aesthetic contemplation he neither understood nor desired" – Nick Carraway’s meditation on the first Dutch sailors and the lost promise of America (Chapter 9)
quote_zh: Fitzgerald uses ‘aesthetic’ to name a moment of pure, disinterested beauty—a contemplation that is pre‑philosophical, almost involuntary. The word suggests that the American continent was once an object of awe untainted by commerce or greed. This moment of aesthetic arrest becomes the novel’s moral benchmark, the standard by which Gatsby’s corrupted, commodified dream is measured. Gatsby confused aesthetic enchantment (Daisy’s voice, the green light) with something attainable and lasting, and in doing so turned art into a transaction.
ex_en: Gatsby’s mansion was an aesthetic triumph that would have moved a connoisseur, but it was built for an audience of one who preferred simpler charms.
ex_zh: The old painter’s final canvas was an aesthetic cry against the darkness, a riot of color that refused to fade.

def_en: corresponding in size or degree; in proportion
def_zh: commensurate with, commensurate reward, commensurate response
quote_en: "for a transitory enchanted moment man must have held his breath in the presence of this continent, compelled into an aesthetic contemplation he neither understood nor desired, face to face for the last time in history with something commensurate to his capacity for wonder." – Nick Carraway’s final reflection on the lost promise of the New World (Chapter 9)
quote_zh: The novel’s penultimate word, ‘commensurate,’ is a term of precise measurement that clashes powerfully with the ineffable wonder it describes. Fitzgerald uses this tension to suggest that the American continent once offered an experience equal to human longing—a perfect fit between desire and object. That commensurability is now lost; Gatsby’s colossal dream is too large for Daisy, and the green light recedes forever. The word ends the novel on a note of profound, mathematically exact loss.
ex_en: Gatsby sought a love commensurate with his colossal imagination, but Daisy was only a mortal woman.
ex_zh: The depth of the old well was commensurate with the sky it reflected, a perfect circle of dark matching a perfect circle of light.
